hero.introParagraph: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric acne (acne vulgaris, ICD-10 L70.0) by secure video visit for children ages 12 to 17. TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. A parent or legal guardian must be present and provide consent for every visit. Following American Academy of Dermatology guidance, TeleDirectMD always pairs topical clindamycin with benzoyl peroxide and never prescribes topical antibiotics as monotherapy, to limit antibiotic resistance, and does not prescribe isotretinoin (Accutane). Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

howItWorks.sectionTitle: How Online Pediatric Acne Treatment Works

steps.title: Confirm eligibility and book
steps.description: Verify the child is ages 12 to 17 and located in one of our 41 licensed states or Washington, DC, then book a video visit and complete the intake form. Note how long acne has been present, which areas are affected, prior treatments tried, current medications, and any allergies.

steps.title: Parent consent and ID verification
steps.description: A parent or legal guardian provides consent and verifies their identity at the start of the visit. The guardian must be present for the entire visit, which is required in every state for a minor's care.

steps.title: MD video evaluation
steps.description: A licensed physician (MD), never a nurse practitioner or physician assistant, evaluates the child by secure video, reviews history and any uploaded photos, and asks targeted questions about the acne to assess type and severity.

steps.title: Treatment plan and prescription
steps.description: If appropriate, the physician sends a prescription to your pharmacy and provides a written visit summary with follow-up guidance. Following AAD guidance, topical clindamycin is always paired with benzoyl peroxide, and isotretinoin is never prescribed.

telehealthRegulations.sectionTitle: Telehealth Regulations Across Our Licensed States
paragraphs: TeleDirectMD operates only where its physicians hold active licensure, currently 41 states plus Washington, DC. Each state sets its own telemedicine standards, and in every state a parent or legal guardian must consent to a minor's care. TeleDirectMD verifies that the child is physically located in a licensed state at the time of the visit; care is not provided to children outside the licensed footprint.

Some states have specific telehealth rules for prescription dermatology medications used in adolescent acne care. State-specific pages cite the controlling state statute. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

paragraphs: Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous (hair-follicle and oil-gland) units. In adolescents, rising androgen levels increase sebum production, follicular cells stick together and plug the pore, and the bacterium Cutibacterium acnes drives inflammation. This produces comedones (blackheads and whiteheads), inflammatory papules and pustules, and in more severe cases nodules.

Teen acne is extremely common and, when treated early, is highly responsive to topical therapy. Per the AAD 2024 acne guidelines, a combination of a topical retinoid with benzoyl peroxide is the recommended first-line regimen.

TeleDirectMD focuses on mild to moderate acne in teens ages 12 to 17 that is well-suited for photo-based telehealth assessment, with a parent present, and refers severe nodulocystic or scarring acne, or cases that may require isotretinoin, to in-person dermatology.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric acne in children ages 12 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Hormonal changes of puberty:
items.text: rising androgen levels increase oil (sebum) production, which is the main driver of adolescent acne.

items.label: Abnormal follicular keratinization:
items.text: excess keratin plugs the follicle and forms comedones.

items.label: Cutibacterium acnes overgrowth:
items.text: bacteria within the follicle drive inflammation.

items.label: Family history:
items.text: a strong family history of acne predicts earlier onset and greater severity.

items.label: Friction or occlusion (acne mechanica):
items.text: sports equipment, helmets, or backpacks can worsen acne in active teens.

items.label: Medications and diet:
items.text: certain medications, and in some teens a high-glycemic diet, can contribute, though diet is a contributor rather than a sole cause.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every breakout is acne vulgaris. Rosacea, folliculitis, perioral dermatitis, and keratosis pilaris can mimic acne. TeleDirectMD uses photo review and clinical history to distinguish acne from look-alike conditions and directs atypical presentations to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Acne vs Rosacea
compareCards.text: Acne vulgaris presents with comedones (blackheads and whiteheads), papules, and pustules and is common in adolescence. Rosacea causes central-face redness and flushing without comedones and is uncommon in teens. The presence or absence of comedones is one of the most reliable distinguishing features.

compareCards.title: Acne vs Folliculitis and Keratosis Pilaris
compareCards.text: Folliculitis appears as uniform pustules centered on hair follicles, often after shaving or occlusion. Keratosis pilaris causes rough chicken-skin bumps on the upper arms and cheeks without inflammation. Neither produces true comedones, which helps separate them from acne vulgaris.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If your child's skin condition does not match typical acne vulgaris or does not respond to standard treatment, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person dermatology evaluation.

treatmentOptions.intro: Most teen acne responds to a topical regimen built around a retinoid plus benzoyl peroxide. TeleDirectMD physicians tailor strength and combination to the acne type and the teen's skin tolerance, and review technique, expected timeline, and sun protection. Following AAD guidance, topical clindamycin is always paired with benzoyl peroxide, and isotretinoin is never prescribed.

sections.title: Comedonal acne
sections.text: First-line treatment is a topical retinoid such as tretinoin, often combined with benzoyl peroxide. Retinoids normalize follicular keratinization and prevent new comedones, while benzoyl peroxide reduces Cutibacterium acnes and limits resistance.

sections.title: Mild to moderate inflammatory acne
sections.text: A topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide foundation is used, with topical clindamycin added when appropriate. Clindamycin is always paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit antibiotic resistance, per AAD guidance. The Twyneo formulation (tretinoin plus benzoyl peroxide) is FDA-labeled from age 9, and fixed clindamycin-benzoyl peroxide products such as Onexton and Acanya are labeled from age 12.

sections.title: Hormonal acne in select female teens
sections.text: For select adolescent females with a hormonal pattern, spironolactone may be used off-label alongside topical therapy. It is not used in males and is not appropriate for every patient.

sections.title: Severe or refractory acne
sections.text: Severe nodulocystic or scarring acne that may need isotretinoin is referred to in-person dermatology. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe isotretinoin because it requires the FDA iPLEDGE program, laboratory monitoring, and in-person oversight.

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Wash affected areas twice daily with a gentle, non-soap cleanser; scrubbing worsens acne.
Apply topical medication to the whole affected zone, not just visible spots.
Expect 6 to 12 weeks before meaningful improvement; consistency matters more than intensity.
Use a non-comedogenic moisturizer and daily SPF 30 or higher, since retinoids increase sun sensitivity.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: A mild initial flare or early worsening can occur with retinoids and does not mean treatment is failing.
If irritation is severe (painful redness, cracking, or blistering), reduce frequency or contact your provider.
If a widespread rash, hives, or swelling develops, stop the medication and seek care.
Follow up by video if there is no improvement after 8 to 12 weeks for a regimen adjustment.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Do not pick or squeeze lesions, as this drives scarring.
Switch to non-comedogenic makeup, sunscreen, and moisturizer products.
Change pillowcases frequently and clean items that touch the face.
After acne clears, continue a maintenance topical retinoid to prevent relapse, per AAD guidance.
If acne is not improving after 12 weeks of consistent treatment, follow up or seek dermatology referral.

items.question: Can a teenager get acne treatment online from TeleDirectMD?
items.answer: Yes. TeleDirectMD treats acne vulgaris (ICD-10 L70.0) by video visit for teens ages 12 to 17 with a parent or legal guardian present and consenting. An MD reviews photos and history, then prescribes topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, or clindamycin paired with benzoyl peroxide. The self-pay visit is $79, and treatment is available in 41 states plus Washington, DC.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD prescribe Accutane (isotretinoin) for teen acne?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe isotretinoin (Accutane) for any patient, including teens ages 12 to 17, because it requires the FDA iPLEDGE program, monthly monitoring, and in-person oversight. Teens with severe nodulocystic or scarring acne who may need isotretinoin are referred to in-person dermatology. We focus on topical therapy and, for select female patients, off-label spironolactone.

items.question: What acne medications can TeleDirectMD prescribe for a 14-year-old?
items.answer: TeleDirectMD physicians can prescribe FDA-labeled topical acne medications for teens ages 12 to 17, including tretinoin (Retin-A Micro, labeled for ages 12+), clindamycin 1% (ages 12+), fixed clindamycin-benzoyl peroxide combinations such as Onexton, and over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide. Clindamycin is always paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit antibiotic resistance, per American Academy of Dermatology guidance.

items.question: Why does TeleDirectMD always pair clindamycin with benzoyl peroxide for acne?
items.answer: Because pairing reduces antibiotic resistance. Following American Academy of Dermatology guidance, TeleDirectMD never prescribes topical clindamycin alone for teens ages 12 to 17; it is always combined with benzoyl peroxide, which suppresses Cutibacterium acnes and the development of resistant strains. This stewardship rule applies to every acne visit across the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD operates.

items.question: How long does teen acne take to improve with treatment?
items.answer: Most teen acne takes 6 to 12 weeks of consistent topical treatment to improve meaningfully, and benefit continues with ongoing use. TeleDirectMD physicians counsel teens ages 12 to 17 and their parents that consistency matters more than intensity, that early worsening can occur with retinoids, and to follow up by video if there is no improvement after 8 to 12 weeks for a regimen adjustment.

items.question: Is online acne treatment appropriate for my child, or should we see a dermatologist?
items.answer: For mild-to-moderate comedonal and inflammatory acne, online treatment through TeleDirectMD is appropriate for teens ages 12 to 17 with a parent present. Children with severe nodulocystic acne, extensive scarring, or signs of a hormonal disorder should see an in-person dermatologist, since those cases may require isotretinoin or laboratory workup that telehealth cannot provide.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for a teen acne visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any teen ages 12 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD. The guardian's identity is verified, and the teen must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the video visit.

items.question: How much does an online teen acne visit cost at TeleDirectMD?
items.answer: An online teen acne visit at TeleDirectMD costs $79 self-pay, with no insurance required, for teens ages 12 to 17. TeleDirectMD is in-network with Aetna, select Blue Cross Blue Shield plans, and UnitedHealthcare where applicable. It is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat acne on the back and chest, not just the face?
items.answer: Yes. TeleDirectMD physicians treat acne vulgaris on the face, chest, and back for teens ages 12 to 17, since the same topical regimens of retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, and clindamycin-benzoyl peroxide combinations apply. Truncal acne may need larger product quantities. Severe or scarring truncal acne that might require isotretinoin is referred to in-person dermatology.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD treat acne in children under 12?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD treats acne only for teens ages 12 to 17, because the standard topical agents (tretinoin and clindamycin) are FDA-labeled from age 12 and most pediatric acne presenting before age 12 warrants in-person evaluation. Children under 12 with acne, or with very early-onset acne suggesting a hormonal cause, are referred for in-person pediatric or dermatology assessment.

paragraphs: This page is informational and is not a substitute for in-person medical care. TeleDirectMD treats children ages 12 to 17 for acne; we do not treat children under age 5 for any condition (ages 0 to 4 are excluded). A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent, and the child must be physically located in a licensed state (41 states plus Washington, DC) at the time of the visit.

TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances or isotretinoin, does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions or ADHD, and does not make new asthma diagnoses. Any infant under 3 months with fever requires emergency care. TeleDirectMD is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.
